question: A wave travelling along a rope is best described as
opt_a: a permanent transfer of rope material from one end to the other
opt_b: a force that exists only at the point where the rope is held
opt_c: a particle that leaves the rope and moves forward
opt_d: a disturbance that moves through the rope while carrying energy
explanation: A wave is a travelling disturbance. In a rope wave, different parts of the rope move from their mean positions, but the rope as a whole does not travel along with the wave. The disturbance carries energy from one place to another. The material particles of the medium only take part in local motion around their equilibrium positions. This is why wave motion is different from throwing an object from one place to another. The central idea is energy transfer through a disturbance, not permanent transport of the medium.

question: A cork floating on water moves up and down as ripples pass across the surface. The ripples travel outward, but the cork does not travel outward with them. This observation mainly shows that
opt_a: water ripples move only matter and transfer no energy
opt_b: the cork and water surface remain completely at rest
opt_c: waves can exist only when the water is very deep
opt_d: disturbance moves while water is not transported
explanation: The cork follows the local motion of the water surface near its position. It oscillates up and down as the disturbance passes, but it does not move along with the outward spread of the ripple. This shows the difference between wave propagation and bulk motion of matter. The wave carries energy across the surface, while the water particles mainly oscillate near their mean positions. A floating object may drift slightly due to other effects, but that is not the basic wave motion being described. The observation separates travelling disturbance from permanent transport of water.

question: In basic wave language, the quantity \(y\) in a displacement wave usually represents
opt_a: displacement of a particle from its mean position
opt_b: distance travelled by the whole medium during the wave
opt_c: speed of the source as it produces the disturbance
opt_d: total mass transported by the wave
explanation: In a displacement wave, \(y\) commonly denotes the displacement of a particle of the medium from its equilibrium or mean position. It is not the distance travelled by the wave itself. The position along the direction of propagation is usually represented by \(x\), while time is represented by \(t\). The wave may move forward, but a medium particle is described by its displacement \(y\) at a given \(x\) and \(t\). This distinction becomes important later when reading equations such as \(y(x,t)\). Confusing \(y\) with the distance travelled by the wave hides the difference between particle motion and wave motion.

question: The pair that represents a wave quantity and its usual SI unit is
explanation: Time period \(T\) is the time taken for one complete oscillation, so its SI unit is \(\text{s}\). Frequency \(f\) is measured in \(\text{Hz}\), not in \(\text{m}\). Wavelength \(\lambda\) is a length, so it is measured in \(\text{m}\), not in \(\text{s}\). Wave speed \(v\) is measured in \(\text{m s}^{-1}\), not in \(\text{Hz}\). The symbols are useful only when their physical meanings and units are kept together. A unit mismatch usually means the wave quantity has been identified wrongly.

question: A disturbance moves through air from a vibrating tuning fork to a listener. During this process, the air particles
opt_a: move permanently from the fork to the listener
opt_b: oscillate about their mean positions while energy travels
opt_c: remain completely at rest because only sound energy moves
opt_d: travel faster than the disturbance in the direction of sound
explanation: Sound in air is produced by disturbances of pressure and density. The air particles do not move permanently from the source to the listener. They oscillate about their mean positions and pass the disturbance to neighbouring particles. The energy of the sound wave travels through the air because of these local oscillations. If air itself moved bodily from the source to the listener, sound would be a bulk flow rather than a wave. The particle motion is local, while the disturbance moves through the medium.

question: The amplitude \(A\) of a wave refers to
opt_a: the distance between two neighbouring crests
opt_b: the number of oscillations per second
opt_c: the time taken for one complete oscillation
opt_d: maximum displacement from the mean position
explanation: Amplitude \(A\) measures the largest displacement of a particle of the medium from its mean position. It tells how far the particle moves on either side of equilibrium during the oscillation. The distance between neighbouring crests is wavelength \(\lambda\), not amplitude. The number of oscillations per second is frequency \(f\), while the time for one oscillation is time period \(T\). Amplitude is therefore a measure of the size of the disturbance. It should not be confused with the distance over which the wave pattern repeats.

question:
Use the graph description below.
A snapshot of a water wave is drawn as displacement \(y\) against position \(x\). Two nearest crests are marked on the curve.
The horizontal distance between these two nearest crests gives
explanation: In a displacement-position graph, the horizontal axis gives position \(x\). The distance between two nearest points in the same phase is the wavelength \(\lambda\). Two nearest crests are in the same phase because both represent maximum positive displacement in the same stage of oscillation. Amplitude \(A\) would be read vertically from the mean line to a crest. Time period \(T\) and frequency \(f\) are time-related quantities, so they are not directly measured as horizontal distances on a \(y-x\) snapshot. A spatial graph gives the pattern in space at one instant.

question: The statement “frequency is \(20\,\text{Hz}\)” means that
explanation: Frequency \(f\) is the number of complete oscillations per unit time. The unit \(\text{Hz}\) means \(\text{s}^{-1}\), so \(20\,\text{Hz}\) means \(20\) oscillations every \(1\,\text{s}\). It does not directly state the wavelength or wave speed. The time taken for one oscillation is the time period \(T\), and it is related by \(f=\frac{1}{T}\). Thus, a larger frequency means more oscillations in the same time interval. The unit \(\text{Hz}\) should be read as a rate of repetition, not as a length or speed.

question:
Match the basic wave symbols with their meanings.
SymbolMeaning
P. \(A\)1. Time for one complete oscillation
Q. \(\lambda\)2. Maximum displacement from mean position
R. \(T\)3. Distance between nearest points in the same phase
S. \(f\)4. Number of oscillations per second
explanation: Amplitude \(A\) is the maximum displacement from the mean position, so P matches \(2\). Wavelength \(\lambda\) is the distance between nearest points in the same phase, so Q matches \(3\). Time period \(T\) is the time for one complete oscillation, so R matches \(1\). Frequency \(f\) is the number of oscillations per second, so S matches \(4\). These four quantities form the first language needed for describing wave motion. The main separation is that \(A\) and \(\lambda\) describe size in displacement or space, while \(T\) and \(f\) describe repetition in time.

question: A particle of a medium completes one oscillation in \(0.020\,\text{s}\). What is the frequency of the wave motion at that point?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Time period \(T=0.020\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Frequency \(f\).
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[
f=\frac{1}{T}
\]
This relation applies because frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
f=\frac{1}{0.020\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Writing the decimal clearly:} \)
\[
0.020=\frac{20}{1000}=\frac{1}{50}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
f=50\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit conversion:} \)
\[
1\,\text{s}^{-1}=1\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The frequency is \(50\,\text{Hz}\).
Taking \(0.020\,\text{s}\) itself as the frequency would interchange \(T\) and \(f\), which are reciprocal quantities.

question: The unit \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) is naturally associated with
explanation: Wave speed \(v\) tells how fast the disturbance travels through space, so it is measured as distance per unit time. The SI unit of distance is \(\text{m}\), and the SI unit of time is \(\text{s}\), giving \(\text{m s}^{-1}\). Amplitude \(A\) and wavelength \(\lambda\) are both lengths, so their unit is \(\text{m}\). Frequency \(f\) is measured in \(\text{Hz}\) or \(\text{s}^{-1}\). The unit itself helps identify the physical role of the quantity. A speed unit should point to propagation, not to the size or repetition rate of oscillation.

question: In the relation \(v=f\lambda\), the symbol \(v\) represents
opt_a: maximum speed of one oscillating particle about its mean position
opt_b: vertical displacement of a particle from equilibrium
opt_c: number of oscillations made by the source in one second
opt_d: propagation speed of the wave disturbance
explanation: The relation \(v=f\lambda\) connects the speed of the travelling wave with its frequency and wavelength. Here \(v\) is the propagation speed of the disturbance, not the speed of an individual medium particle during oscillation. A medium particle may move up and down or back and forth, depending on the wave type. The disturbance, however, moves from one region of the medium to another. Frequency \(f\) gives how often oscillations repeat, and wavelength \(\lambda\) gives the spatial repeat distance. The symbol \(v\) in this relation belongs to the travelling pattern, not to the local oscillatory motion of a particle.

question:
Assertion: A wave can carry energy from one place to another without permanent transport of matter.
Reason: In a mechanical wave, particles of the medium generally oscillate about their mean positions.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true because wave motion is a way of transferring energy through a disturbance. In a mechanical wave, the material particles of the medium do not need to move permanently from the source to the receiver. They usually oscillate around mean positions and pass the disturbance to neighbouring particles. That local oscillation is the reason the disturbance can travel while the medium itself is not transported bodily. The Reason therefore gives the physical explanation of the Assertion. The idea is especially clear in rope waves, water ripples, and sound waves in air.

question: A stone thrown across a field and a ripple moving across water both involve motion. The motion of the stone is not a wave mainly because
opt_a: the stone has no energy while moving
opt_b: the stone material itself is transported
opt_c: water can never show particle motion
opt_d: a wave must always be visible to the eye
explanation: A thrown stone is an object moving bodily from one place to another. Its material itself is transported through space. A water ripple, in contrast, is a travelling disturbance of the water surface. The water particles mainly move locally while the wave pattern moves outward. Wave motion is identified by propagation of a disturbance, not by any motion whatsoever. The example of a thrown stone helps separate object motion from wave motion. Energy travels in both cases, but the mechanism of transport is different.

question:
Study the table and choose the row with a mismatched unit.
RowQuantityUnit
PAmplitude \(A\)\(\text{m}\)
QTime period \(T\)\(\text{s}\)
RFrequency \(f\)\(\text{Hz}\)
SWavelength \(\lambda\)\(\text{s}^{-1}\)
explanation: Wavelength \(\lambda\) is a distance, so its SI unit is \(\text{m}\). The unit \(\text{s}^{-1}\) belongs to frequency \(f\), and it is also written as \(\text{Hz}\). Row P is matched properly because amplitude \(A\) is also a displacement and is measured in \(\text{m}\). Row Q is proper because time period \(T\) is measured in \(\text{s}\). Row R is proper because frequency \(f\) is measured in \(\text{Hz}\). The mismatched row confuses a spatial repeat distance with a time-rate quantity.

question: A wave has frequency \(25\,\text{Hz}\) and wavelength \(0.40\,\text{m}\). What is its wave speed?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Frequency \(f=25\,\text{Hz}=25\,\text{s}^{-1}\), wavelength \(\lambda=0.40\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wave speed \(v\).
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
This relation applies because the wave travels one wavelength in one time period, and \(f=\frac{1}{T}\).
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=(25\,\text{s}^{-1})(0.40\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
25\times0.40=10
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \)
\[
\text{s}^{-1}\times\text{m}=\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is \(10\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Dividing \(f\) by \(\lambda\) would give a unit \(\text{s}^{-1}\text{m}^{-1}\), which is not a speed.

question:
Two statements about a simple travelling wave are given.
I. The medium particles may oscillate even when the wave pattern travels forward.
II. The wave speed always means the same thing as the instantaneous speed of a medium particle.
III. The wavelength is a spatial separation between nearest points in the same phase.
The supported statements are
explanation: Statement I is supported because particles of a medium can oscillate locally while the wave disturbance travels forward. This is a basic feature of mechanical wave motion. Statement II is not supported because wave speed describes propagation of the disturbance, while particle speed describes local motion of a particle of the medium. These two speeds are physically different quantities. Statement III is supported because wavelength \(\lambda\) is the distance between nearest points that are in the same phase, such as neighbouring crests. The combination keeps particle motion, wave motion, and spatial repetition separate.

question: A sinusoidal wave is observed at one fixed point. The particle at that point returns to the same displacement and same direction of motion every \(0.10\,\text{s}\). The quantity \(0.10\,\text{s}\) is the
explanation: At one fixed point, the motion being observed is the oscillation of a single medium particle. The time taken for that particle to return to the same state of motion is the time period \(T\). The phrase “same displacement and same direction of motion” indicates one complete oscillation. Wavelength \(\lambda\) is measured in space, not in time. Wave speed \(v\) tells how fast the disturbance travels, while amplitude \(A\) tells the maximum displacement. A time reading from one fixed point is naturally connected with \(T\), not with the spatial separation \(\lambda\).

question: A wave travels along a long spring. One coil of the spring is observed carefully as the disturbance passes. The coil should be expected to
opt_a: move from the source end to the far end with the disturbance
opt_b: remain fixed at its mean position at every instant
opt_c: oscillate near its mean position as the disturbance passes
opt_d: become the source of a new material stream through the spring
explanation: In a mechanical wave, the particles of the medium take part in local oscillatory motion. For a spring wave, each coil moves about its mean position as the disturbance passes through it. The disturbance can travel from one end to the other without the same coil being transported along the entire spring. The coil is not permanently carried with the wave pattern. It is also not motionless, because the wave requires local disturbance of the medium. This separates motion of medium particles from propagation of the wave disturbance.

question: The quantity that tells how many complete oscillations occur in \(1\,\text{s}\) is
explanation: Frequency \(f\) counts the number of complete oscillations per second. Its SI unit is \(\text{Hz}\), which is the same as \(\text{s}^{-1}\). Wavelength \(\lambda\) measures spatial repetition, not time repetition. Amplitude \(A\) measures the maximum displacement from the mean position. Wave speed \(v\) tells how fast the disturbance travels through the medium. The phrase “per second” is the clue that the quantity is a rate of oscillation, not a length or displacement.

question: A sound wave reaches a listener through air. The wave propagation direction is from the source toward the listener. In the basic particle-motion picture, air particles mainly
opt_a: drift steadily from the source to the listener
opt_b: oscillate about mean positions while sound travels
opt_c: move only upward and downward in all sound waves
opt_d: stay permanently compressed after the sound has passed
explanation: Sound in air is a mechanical wave, so it needs the particles of air to transmit the disturbance. The particles do not travel bodily from the source to the listener. Instead, they oscillate about their mean positions and pass the disturbance to neighbouring layers of air. The sound energy moves through the medium because of this local motion. A permanent drift of air would be a wind-like flow, not the basic description of sound propagation. After the disturbance passes, the particles return to their ordinary oscillatory state around equilibrium.

question: In a displacement wave, the pair \(x\) and \(t\) is used because the displacement of a medium particle may depend on
explanation: A travelling wave is not described by displacement alone. The displacement of a particle depends on where the particle is located and at what instant it is observed. The coordinate \(x\) specifies position along the direction of propagation, while \(t\) specifies time. That is why a wave displacement is often written as \(y(x,t)\). The same particle may have different displacements at different times, and different particles may have different displacements at the same time. This two-variable dependence is a basic reason wave motion is richer than the motion of a single oscillator.

question:
Use the graph description below.
At a fixed instant, a wave on a string is represented by a displacement \(y\) versus position \(x\) curve. The curve has a highest point, a lowest point, and a central mean line.
The vertical distance from the mean line to the highest point represents
explanation: On a displacement-position graph, the vertical coordinate gives displacement \(y\). The maximum displacement from the mean line is the amplitude \(A\). The highest point on the curve is a crest, and the vertical distance from the mean position to that crest gives \(A\). Wavelength \(\lambda\) is a horizontal distance between nearest points in the same phase, such as neighbouring crests. Time period \(T\) and frequency \(f\) require time information, not just the shape of a spatial snapshot. Reading amplitude vertically prevents it from being confused with the horizontal spacing of the wave pattern.

question: A water ripple spreads outward on a pond after a small stone is dropped. A leaf floating near one place rises and falls but remains nearly at the same place. The best interpretation is
opt_a: the ripple carries energy while water moves locally
opt_b: the leaf proves that no wave energy is being transferred
opt_c: the water at the leaf must travel all the way to the pond edge
opt_d: the ripple is a moving object rather than a disturbance
explanation: The spreading ripple is a travelling disturbance on the water surface. The floating leaf shows the local motion of water near that point, not the transport of the same water all the way outward. The wave can carry energy away from the point of disturbance while the medium particles move mainly around their mean positions. A lack of large outward leaf motion does not mean there is no energy transfer. It means the energy transfer is happening through the wave disturbance rather than through bulk transport of water. This is one of the simplest visual ways to distinguish wave propagation from matter transport.

question:
The following table lists a few motions. Select the row that best represents wave motion rather than ordinary object transport.
RowObservationNature of motion
PA ball flies from one player to anotherThe object itself is transported
QA ripple spreads on waterA disturbance travels through the medium
RA car moves along a straight roadThe body changes position as a whole
SA stone falls freely downwardThe object itself moves through space
explanation: Row Q describes a ripple spreading on water, which is a travelling disturbance. The water surface particles take part in local motion, while the ripple pattern moves outward. In rows P, R, and S, the described object itself is transported from one place to another. Such motion may involve energy, but it is not wave motion in the basic sense. Wave motion is identified by disturbance propagation through a medium or space. The key separation is between a moving object and a moving pattern of disturbance.

question: For a wave with speed \(12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and frequency \(3.0\,\text{Hz}\), the wavelength is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Wave speed \(v=12\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), frequency \(f=3.0\,\text{Hz}=3.0\,\text{s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wavelength \(\lambda\).
\( \textbf{Relation choice:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
This relation connects propagation speed, temporal repetition, and spatial repetition of a periodic wave.
\( \textbf{Rearranging for wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda=\frac{v}{f}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda=\frac{12\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{3.0\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda=4.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \)
\[
\frac{\text{m s}^{-1}}{\text{s}^{-1}}=\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength is \(4.0\,\text{m}\).
Multiplying \(v\) and \(f\) would give \(\text{m s}^{-2}\), which is not the unit of wavelength.

question: A wave on a string travels to the right. At one instant, a small marked point on the string is moving upward. This information alone shows that
opt_a: the marked point must move to the right with the wave
opt_b: the point’s motion need not match the wave direction
opt_c: the wave cannot carry energy along the string
opt_d: the string has no particle motion at that point
explanation: A travelling wave has two different kinds of motion to keep separate. The wave pattern may travel to the right, while a marked point of the string can move upward or downward at a given instant. The motion of the point is particle motion about its mean position. The motion of the pattern is wave propagation along the string. These directions need not be the same, especially for transverse waves. Observing a point moving upward does not mean the point is being carried to the right with the wave.

question:
Two statements are made about wave motion.
I. A wave may transfer energy from one region to another.
II. The material medium must always be permanently transported with the wave.
III. In a mechanical wave, particles of the medium can oscillate about equilibrium positions.
The statements that fit the basic wave model are
explanation: Statement I is true because energy transfer is a central feature of wave motion. Statement III is also true for mechanical waves, where particles of the medium usually oscillate about their equilibrium positions. Statement II is not true because a wave does not require permanent transport of the material medium. A rope wave can travel along the rope even though each small part of the rope moves locally. A sound wave can reach a listener without air from the source travelling all the way to the listener. The false statement confuses wave propagation with bulk motion of matter.

question:
Read the passage and answer the question.
A long rope is tied at one end. The other end is shaken once, producing a pulse that travels along the rope. A small coloured mark on the rope moves up and down as the pulse passes and then returns close to its original position.
What does the coloured mark help identify?
opt_a: the speed of the source alone
opt_b: the permanent transport of rope material
opt_c: the local motion of a medium particle
opt_d: the conversion of the rope into empty space
explanation: The coloured mark represents a particular small part of the rope. As the pulse passes, that part of the rope is displaced and then returns close to its original position. This shows local particle motion in the medium. The pulse itself travels along the rope, but the marked portion does not travel along with the pulse to the far end. The source starts the disturbance, but the mark is used to observe the motion of the medium at one location. The example makes the difference between a travelling pulse and the motion of a material point on the rope clear.

question: In a wave on a string, a student records that the pulse takes \(0.50\,\text{s}\) to travel \(2.0\,\text{m}\) along the string. During the same interval, a marked point on the string only moves up and down. What is the speed of the pulse?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Distance travelled by the pulse \(=2.0\,\text{m}\), time taken \(=0.50\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Speed of the pulse along the string.
\( \textbf{Relation used:} \)
\[
\text{speed}=\frac{\text{distance travelled by disturbance}}{\text{time taken}}
\]
This relation is applied to the travelling pulse, not to the up-and-down motion of the marked point.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\frac{2.0\,\text{m}}{0.50\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v=4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Particle-motion check:} \) The marked point moving up and down does not change the distance travelled by the pulse.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The pulse speed is \(4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Using the vertical distance moved by the mark would describe particle motion, not propagation speed along the string.

question: In a mechanical wave, “particle velocity” and “wave velocity” are not the same because
opt_a: particle velocity is local motion; wave velocity is disturbance motion
opt_b: particle velocity is always zero, while wave velocity is always infinite
opt_c: particle velocity exists only in vacuum, while wave velocity exists only in solids
opt_d: particle velocity and wave velocity always have the same magnitude and direction
explanation: Particle velocity describes how a particular particle of the medium is moving at an instant. Wave velocity describes how fast the disturbance or wave pattern travels through the medium. These two quantities can differ in direction and magnitude. For example, in a transverse wave on a string, a point on the string may move up or down while the wave travels horizontally. Particle velocity can change during oscillation, whereas wave speed in a uniform medium may remain constant. Treating them as the same removes the distinction between the material point and the travelling pattern.

question:
Assertion: In a transverse wave on a string, a marked point on the string need not move in the same direction as the wave travels.
Reason: The wave motion of the disturbance and the local motion of the string particle are different aspects of the same wave phenomenon.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true because a transverse wave on a string can travel horizontally while each string particle moves perpendicular to that direction. A marked point on the string therefore need not travel along with the wave pattern. The Reason is also true because wave propagation and particle oscillation are two different parts of wave description. The travelling disturbance carries energy along the string, while the string particles execute local motion. This difference explains why the marked point’s motion can have a direction different from the direction of wave travel. The statement would fail only if one wrongly treated the string particle as the travelling wave itself.

question:
Use the arrangement described below.
A long horizontal string has three coloured points P, Q, and R fixed on it. A pulse is sent from the left end toward the right. As the pulse reaches each coloured point, the point rises and then falls back near its original position.
The motion of P, Q, and R most directly shows that
opt_a: the string material flows continuously to the right
opt_b: each small part of the string oscillates locally
opt_c: the pulse loses all energy before reaching Q
opt_d: the coloured points become independent waves
explanation:
\(\textbf{Observation:}\) Each coloured point rises and then falls back near its original position as the pulse passes.
\(\textbf{Particle motion:}\) Each coloured point represents a small part of the string.
\(\textbf{Wave motion:}\) The pulse travels from left to right along the string.
\(\textbf{Key distinction:}\) The string material itself is not carried continuously to the right with the pulse.
\(\textbf{Energy transfer:}\) The disturbance carries energy along the string through local oscillations of the string particles.
\(\textbf{Final answer:}\) The motion shows that each small part of the string oscillates locally.

question: A claim says: “If a wave travels from left to right, every particle of the medium must also move from left to right permanently.” The best correction is that
opt_a: particles oscillate locally while the disturbance travels
opt_b: wave motion cannot occur in a material medium
opt_c: a wave has no connection with particle motion
opt_d: the wave must stop if particles are not permanently transported
explanation: The claim confuses wave propagation with permanent motion of matter. In many mechanical waves, particles of the medium oscillate about their mean positions. The disturbance travels from one region to another as neighbouring particles interact. This allows energy to be transmitted without the same material particles moving permanently with the wave. Particle motion is still essential in a mechanical wave, but it is local rather than bulk transport. A wave can therefore move left to right even when particles only oscillate around equilibrium positions.

question: In a wave on a rope, the wave speed is \(6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). At one instant, a small part of the rope has an upward particle velocity of \(0.30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The most careful comparison is
opt_a: the two speeds must be added to get \(6.30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
opt_b: wave speed and particle velocity describe different motions
opt_c: the wave speed must become \(0.30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
opt_d: the particle velocity must always equal \(6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) Wave speed along the rope is \(6.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), and local particle velocity at that instant is \(0.30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) upward.
\( \textbf{Meaning of wave speed:} \) It tells how fast the disturbance travels along the rope.
\( \textbf{Meaning of particle velocity:} \) It tells how fast a particular part of the rope is moving about its mean position at that instant.
\( \textbf{Direction comparison:} \) The wave speed is along the rope, while the stated particle velocity is upward.
\( \textbf{Physical decision:} \) Since they refer to different motions, they should not be equated.
\( \textbf{Why addition is unsuitable:} \) Adding them as ordinary speeds would mix propagation speed with local oscillatory speed.
\( \textbf{Why equality is unsuitable:} \) A particle’s velocity can vary during oscillation, but the wave speed in a uniform rope can remain fixed.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed and particle velocity describe different motions.
The numerical values are not competing measurements of the same physical quantity.

question:
The following pairs are used in a wave description. Identify the pair that is most likely to be confused when distinguishing particle motion from wave motion.
PairQuantity 1Quantity 2
PAmplitude \(A\)Maximum displacement
QTime period \(T\)Time for one oscillation
RParticle velocityWave velocity
SFrequency \(f\)Oscillations per second
explanation: Pair R contains particle velocity and wave velocity, which refer to different motions. Particle velocity is the instantaneous velocity of a medium particle as it oscillates. Wave velocity is the speed with which the disturbance propagates through the medium. The other rows pair a quantity with its own meaning rather than two easily confused physical quantities. Amplitude is maximum displacement, time period is time for one oscillation, and frequency is oscillations per second. The main caution is that the word “velocity” appears in both terms, but the objects whose motion is being described are different.

question: A sound wave travelling through air is called a mechanical wave because
opt_a: it can travel through a vacuum
opt_b: it needs a material medium for its propagation
opt_c: it always travels faster than light
opt_d: it transports air permanently from source to listener
explanation: A mechanical wave needs particles of a material medium to transmit the disturbance. Sound in air is produced by pressure and density variations passed from one layer of air to the next. Without air or another material medium, these variations cannot be passed along. This is why sound cannot travel through a vacuum. The wave can still carry energy, but the air particles do not have to be permanently transported from the source to the listener. The word mechanical here points to the need for a medium, not to the motion of a machine.

question: Light from the Sun reaches Earth through mostly empty space. This observation supports the idea that light is
opt_a: a mechanical wave that requires air for propagation
opt_b: a longitudinal sound wave needing a material medium
opt_c: an electromagnetic wave that can travel in vacuum
opt_d: a wave that carries no energy through space
explanation: Light can travel through the vacuum of space, so it cannot be classified as a mechanical wave in the same way as sound or waves on a string. Mechanical waves require a material medium because their propagation depends on the motion of particles of that medium. Electromagnetic waves can propagate even without a material medium. Sunlight reaching Earth is a direct everyday example of this difference. Light still carries energy, even though it does not need air or water for propagation. The absence of a medium separates electromagnetic waves from mechanical waves.

question:
Study the table and identify the classification that is not suitable.
RowWaveClassification
PSound in airMechanical wave
QWave on a stretched stringMechanical wave
RLight in vacuumElectromagnetic wave
SSound in vacuumMechanical wave that propagates normally
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave, but it cannot propagate normally in a vacuum. It needs a material medium such as air, water, or a solid to transmit pressure and density disturbances. Row P is suitable because sound in air is a mechanical wave. Row Q is also suitable because a wave on a stretched string uses the string as its medium. Row R is suitable because light is an electromagnetic wave and can travel in vacuum. Row S mixes a true classification of sound with a false condition for its propagation.

question: A sealed bell jar is slowly evacuated while an electric bell rings inside it. The bell can still be seen vibrating, but its sound becomes weaker and may finally be inaudible. The best reason is that
opt_a: the bell stops transferring energy to its surroundings
opt_b: sound needs a material medium, and air is being removed
opt_c: light needs air for propagation, but sound does not
opt_d: the frequency of the bell becomes zero in a vacuum
explanation: The electric bell can continue to vibrate even when air is removed from the jar. However, sound from the bell needs a material medium to travel to the listener. As the air is removed, fewer air particles are available to carry the pressure disturbance. The sound therefore becomes weaker and may become inaudible. Light from the bell can still travel through the glass and evacuated space, so the bell may still be seen. The situation compares mechanical sound waves with electromagnetic light waves in a direct way.

question:
Two statements about wave types are given.
I. Waves on a stretched string require a material medium.
II. Electromagnetic waves cannot travel in vacuum.
III. Sound waves in air are mechanical waves.
The supported statements are
explanation: Statement I is supported because a wave on a stretched string needs the string as its medium. Statement III is supported because sound in air is transmitted through pressure and density changes of air. Statement II is not supported because electromagnetic waves can travel in vacuum. Light is the usual example of an electromagnetic wave that does not require a material medium. The difference is not whether the wave carries energy, because both types can carry energy. The real separation is the requirement or non-requirement of a material medium.

question: A radio signal from a spacecraft reaches Earth across space, while sound from a ringing bell cannot cross a perfect vacuum. This contrast occurs because
opt_a: radio waves are electromagnetic; sound is mechanical
opt_b: sound has larger amplitude than radio waves
opt_c: radio waves require air, whereas sound requires no medium
opt_d: sound travels only when its wavelength is zero
explanation: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves, so they can propagate through vacuum. Sound is a mechanical wave, so it needs a material medium to carry the disturbance. A perfect vacuum has no particles to transmit compressions and rarefactions of sound. The distinction does not depend simply on amplitude or wavelength. A very loud sound still cannot travel through a perfect vacuum if no medium is present. The spacecraft example shows that not all waves need a material medium.

question:
Match the wave examples with their basic type.
ExampleType
P. Sound in air1. Mechanical wave
Q. Light in vacuum2. Electromagnetic wave
R. Wave on a string3. Mechanical wave
S. Seismic wave through Earth4. Mechanical wave
explanation: Sound in air is a mechanical wave because it needs air particles to transmit the disturbance. Light in vacuum is an electromagnetic wave because it can propagate without a material medium. A wave on a string is mechanical because the string itself is the medium. Seismic waves travel through Earth material, so they are also mechanical waves. The same broad word “wave” includes different physical mechanisms of propagation. The classification depends mainly on whether a material medium is required.

question: A claim says, “If a wave can travel without a material medium, it cannot carry energy.” The best response is that
opt_a: the claim is true for mechanical and electromagnetic waves
opt_b: only medium-based mechanical waves can carry energy
opt_c: electromagnetic waves can transfer energy through vacuum
opt_d: waves in vacuum must have zero frequency and energy
explanation: A wave does not need to be mechanical in order to carry energy. Electromagnetic waves can travel through vacuum and still transfer energy. Sunlight warms Earth even though it has travelled through space where there is no material medium for most of the path. Mechanical waves need a medium, but that is not a general requirement for all energy-carrying waves. The claim wrongly connects energy transport only with matter-particle oscillation. The ability to travel through vacuum is a property of electromagnetic waves, not a sign of zero energy.

question: A wave travels along a horizontal string toward the right. A marked point on the string moves up and down as the wave passes. This wave is transverse because the particle displacement is
opt_d: zero at every point of the string during propagation
explanation: A transverse wave is defined by the direction of particle displacement relative to the direction of wave propagation. Here the wave travels horizontally toward the right, while the marked point moves vertically up and down. These directions are perpendicular to each other. The wave still carries energy along the string, but the string particles do not move along the direction of travel. If the particles moved back and forth parallel to the propagation direction, the wave would be longitudinal instead. The observed rightward wave motion and vertical particle motion identify the transverse nature.

question:
Use the graph description below.
A snapshot of a wave on a stretched string is drawn as displacement \(y\) versus position \(x\). The curve has alternate highest and lowest points as the pattern extends along \(x\).
In this snapshot, the highest and lowest points are respectively called
explanation: In the usual displacement picture of a transverse wave, the highest points are called crests and the lowest points are called troughs. The vertical coordinate \(y\) shows displacement from the mean position. A crest corresponds to maximum positive displacement, while a trough corresponds to maximum negative displacement. Compressions and rarefactions are used mainly for longitudinal waves such as sound in air. Nodes and antinodes belong to standing wave patterns, not to the first description of a travelling transverse wave. The graph vocabulary should match the type of wave representation being used.

question:
The following situation describes a transverse wave on a string.
A pulse moves from left to right along a stretched string. At a particular instant, one small portion of the string is above its mean position and is moving downward.
What can be said about the wave and that portion of the string?
opt_a: The pulse and the string portion must both move left to right
opt_b: The pulse travels along the string, while the portion moves locally
opt_c: The string portion cannot move because the pulse is already moving
opt_d: The pulse must be longitudinal because the string portion moves
explanation: The pulse is the travelling disturbance and it moves along the string from left to right. A particular portion of the string can move up or down as the pulse passes. This local motion is transverse to the direction of propagation. The string portion is not carried permanently to the right with the pulse. Its downward motion at that instant is part of its oscillation about the mean position. The situation is consistent with a transverse wave because particle displacement and wave propagation are perpendicular.

question: In a transverse wave moving along the \(x\)-axis, particle displacement may be along the \(y\)-direction. The relation between these two directions is
opt_b: the \(y\)-direction is the same as the direction of propagation
explanation: For a transverse wave travelling along the \(x\)-axis, the direction of propagation is along \(x\). If the medium particles move along \(y\), their displacement is perpendicular to the direction of propagation. This is the defining feature of a transverse wave. The symbol \(y\) commonly represents displacement of a particle from its mean position, not the distance travelled by the wave. The wave pattern advances along \(x\), while the local particle motion can be along \(y\). Keeping \(x\) and \(y\) separate avoids mixing propagation direction with displacement direction.

question: A row in a notes table says, “Wave on a stretched string: particle displacement parallel to propagation.” The needed correction is
opt_b: a stretched string cannot carry any wave
opt_c: the wave on a string must travel only through vacuum
opt_d: particle displacement is always zero in a string wave
explanation: A common wave on a stretched string is transverse. In such a wave, the disturbance travels along the string, while particles of the string move perpendicular to the direction of travel. Saying that the displacement is parallel describes a longitudinal wave, not a transverse string wave. The string is a material medium and can carry mechanical waves. The particle displacement is not zero; it is the local motion that makes the wave visible. The correction must change the direction relation, not deny the existence of the wave.

question: A transverse wave on a string has amplitude \(2.0\,\text{cm}\). A point of the string is observed at a crest. Its displacement from the mean position at that instant is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) Amplitude \(A=2.0\,\text{cm}\).
\( \textbf{Position described:} \) The point is at a crest.
\( \textbf{Meaning of amplitude:} \) Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the mean position.
\( \textbf{Crest meaning:} \) A crest is the point of maximum positive displacement in the wave profile.
\( \textbf{Displacement at crest:} \)
\[
y=+A
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
y=+2.0\,\text{cm}
\]
\( \textbf{Magnitude asked by options:} \) The displacement from the mean position is \(2.0\,\text{cm}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The displacement is \(2.0\,\text{cm}\).
The value \(4.0\,\text{cm}\) would represent crest-to-trough separation, not displacement from the mean line.

question:
Assertion: A wave on a stretched string is usually represented with crests and troughs.
Reason: In a transverse wave, the displacement of string particles is perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: A wave on a stretched string is commonly transverse. Its particles move perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels. This perpendicular displacement produces a visible profile with parts above and below the mean position. The highest parts are called crests and the lowest parts are called troughs. The Reason therefore gives the physical basis for the usual crest-trough representation. The representation would not be the natural first picture for a longitudinal pressure wave in air.

question: In the description of a transverse wave, the phrase “perpendicular displacement” refers to
opt_a: the distance between two neighbouring crests
opt_b: the time taken by the source to complete one oscillation
opt_c: the speed of the wave relative to the source
opt_d: particle displacement compared with wave direction
explanation: The word perpendicular in a transverse wave compares two directions. One direction is the direction in which the wave disturbance travels. The other is the direction in which particles of the medium are displaced. If these two directions are at right angles, the wave is transverse. This statement does not define wavelength, period, or speed. Wavelength is a distance between points in the same phase, and period is a time interval. The phrase is about geometry of motion, not about how fast or how far the wave repeats.

question: A transverse wave travels along a string from west to east. At a certain point, the string particle is moving north-south. This description is possible because
opt_a: transverse particle motion is perpendicular to wave propagation
opt_b: transverse waves require particle motion parallel to propagation
opt_c: the string particle must be transported eastward permanently
opt_d: a string wave cannot carry energy west to east
explanation: West-east is the direction of propagation of the wave along the string. North-south motion of a string particle is a local displacement direction. These two directions can be perpendicular, so the situation fits a transverse wave. The particle is not required to travel eastward with the wave. The wave disturbance can carry energy along the string while the string particles move across the direction of propagation. Direction wording such as west-east and north-south is a useful way to test the geometry of transverse motion.

question: A transverse wave snapshot shows a crest at position P and the next trough at position Q. If the amplitude is \(A\), the magnitude of the change in displacement from P to Q is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given idea:} \) At a crest, displacement from the mean position is \(+A\).
\( \textbf{Trough displacement:} \) At a trough, displacement from the mean position is \(-A\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Change in displacement from crest P to trough Q.
\( \textbf{Difference calculation:} \)
\[
\Delta y=y_Q-y_P
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution with signs:} \)
\[
\Delta y=(-A)-(+A)=-2A
\]
\( \textbf{Magnitude of change:} \)
\[
|\Delta y|=2A
\]
\( \textbf{Option match:} \) The listed value is the magnitude of the displacement change, \(2A\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The change in displacement from crest to trough is \(2A\).
Using only \(A\) would measure displacement from the mean line to one extreme, not the full crest-to-trough change.

question: A longitudinal wave is travelling through a slinky from left to right. The coils of the slinky move alternately closer together and farther apart. The particle displacement in this wave is mainly
opt_a: perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
opt_b: parallel to the direction of wave propagation
opt_c: opposite to gravity at every point
opt_d: zero because only the wave pattern moves
explanation: In a longitudinal wave, particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. If the wave moves from left to right, the coils of the slinky move back and forth along the same line. Regions where coils come closer are compressions, and regions where they spread apart are rarefactions. The wave pattern travels through the slinky, but each coil has local oscillatory motion. This is different from a transverse string wave, where particles move perpendicular to the direction of propagation. The closeness and separation of coils are direct signs of longitudinal motion.

question: Sound in air is best described as
opt_b: a wave that needs no medium
opt_c: a stream of air particles moving permanently from source to listener
explanation: Sound in air is mechanical because it needs air as a material medium. It is longitudinal because air particles oscillate back and forth parallel to the direction in which the sound travels. The wave consists of successive compressions and rarefactions in air. A compression is a region of higher pressure and density, while a rarefaction is a region of lower pressure and density. Sound is not electromagnetic, and it cannot travel through a perfect vacuum. The air particles take part in local oscillations rather than moving permanently from the source to the listener.

question:
Use the graph description below.
A sound wave in air is represented by a pressure variation graph along the direction of propagation. Point P is at a pressure maximum, and point Q is at the nearest pressure minimum.
Point P and point Q correspond respectively to
opt_c: node and antinode in standing waves
explanation: In a sound wave, pressure variations are a natural way to represent the longitudinal disturbance. A pressure maximum corresponds to a compression, where air particles are closer together and the density is higher. A pressure minimum corresponds to a rarefaction, where air particles are farther apart and the density is lower. Crest and trough are more commonly used for displacement pictures of transverse waves. Nodes and antinodes belong to standing waves, not the first travelling-wave description here. The pressure graph should be read using compression-rarefaction language rather than crest-trough language.

question: A tuning fork vibrates near the open end of a tube filled with air. The disturbance travels down the tube as sound. During this propagation, a small layer of air
opt_a: moves back and forth along the tube
opt_b: moves only perpendicular to the tube
opt_c: travels permanently from the tuning fork to the closed end
opt_d: remains at rest because sound is only pressure
explanation: In air, sound is a longitudinal wave. The air layers oscillate back and forth along the same line in which the sound travels. This motion creates alternate compressions and rarefactions. The pressure disturbance travels down the tube, but the same air layer is not permanently carried from the source to the far end. Pressure variation and particle displacement are linked parts of the wave, so the air layer is not completely at rest. The important direction relation is that the particle motion is along the direction of propagation.

question:
A notes table for longitudinal waves is shown below. Identify the row that gives the best description.
RowParticle motionUsual regions formed
PPerpendicular to propagationCrests and troughs
QParallel to propagationCompressions and rarefactions
RNo particle motionNodes only
SRandom in all directionsOnly crests
explanation: A longitudinal wave is identified by particle motion parallel to the direction of wave propagation. The natural regions formed in such a wave are compressions and rarefactions. Compressions are regions of higher pressure and density, and rarefactions are regions of lower pressure and density. Row P describes a transverse wave more closely because perpendicular particle motion gives crest-trough representation. Row R wrongly removes particle motion, even though mechanical waves need the medium particles to transmit the disturbance. Row S does not describe an organized wave pattern.

question: Two nearest compressions in a sound wave are \(0.80\,\text{m}\) apart. If the frequency of the sound is \(250\,\text{Hz}\), what is the speed of sound in this case?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Distance between nearest compressions \(=0.80\,\text{m}\), frequency \(f=250\,\text{Hz}=250\,\text{s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Wave interpretation:} \) The distance between two nearest compressions is one wavelength.
\[
\lambda=0.80\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wave speed \(v\).
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
This relation applies because one full spatial repeat of a periodic wave is one wavelength.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=(250\,\text{s}^{-1})(0.80\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v=200\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \)
\[
\text{s}^{-1}\times\text{m}=\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The speed of sound in this case is \(200\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The spacing of nearest compressions is not half a wavelength; it is the full spatial repeat of the pressure pattern.

question: In a longitudinal wave travelling along the \(x\)-axis, a particle of the medium is displaced first toward \(+x\) and then toward \(-x\). This description means that the particle
opt_a: oscillates perpendicular to the direction of propagation
opt_b: has no role in carrying the disturbance
opt_c: changes the wave into an electromagnetic wave
opt_d: oscillates parallel to the direction of propagation
explanation: If the wave travels along the \(x\)-axis, then the direction of propagation is along \(x\). A particle displaced toward \(+x\) and \(-x\) is moving back and forth along that same axis. Such motion is parallel to the direction of propagation, so it matches a longitudinal wave. This is the motion found in sound waves in air and compression waves in a spring. The particle does not travel permanently in either direction; it oscillates around its mean position. The sign of displacement changes during oscillation, but the line of motion remains parallel to propagation.

question:
Assertion: In a longitudinal sound wave, compressions are regions of relatively high pressure and high density.
Reason: In a compression, neighbouring air particles are closer together than in their undisturbed state.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true because a compression in a sound wave is a crowded region of the medium. When neighbouring air particles are closer together, the mass of air per unit volume is greater, so the density is higher. The pressure is also higher than in the undisturbed region because the air is locally compressed. The Reason states exactly why a compression has increased density and pressure. Rarefactions show the opposite situation, with particles farther apart and pressure lower than normal. The explanation depends on local crowding of particles, not on permanent air flow.

question: A comparison between transverse and longitudinal waves is needed. The most reliable basis for classification is
opt_a: whether the wave is visible or invisible to an observer
opt_b: whether the wave speed is large or small
opt_c: particle displacement direction relative to propagation
opt_d: the loudness produced by the wave
explanation: Transverse and longitudinal waves are classified by comparing particle displacement with the direction of wave propagation. In a transverse wave, particle displacement is perpendicular to propagation. In a longitudinal wave, particle displacement is parallel to propagation. Visibility is not a reliable basis because many waves are invisible but still have definite type. Speed and loudness also do not define the geometry of particle motion. The classification is therefore based on a direction relation, not on sensory appearance or magnitude.

question:
Match the wave descriptions with the suitable wave type.
DescriptionWave type
P. Particle displacement perpendicular to propagation1. Transverse wave
Q. Particle displacement parallel to propagation2. Longitudinal wave
R. Crests and troughs are the common shape features3. Transverse wave
S. Compressions and rarefactions are formed4. Longitudinal wave
explanation: A transverse wave has particle displacement perpendicular to the direction of propagation, so P matches \(1\). A longitudinal wave has particle displacement parallel to the direction of propagation, so Q matches \(2\). Crests and troughs are the usual shape features in a transverse displacement representation, so R matches \(3\). Compressions and rarefactions are the characteristic regions of a longitudinal wave, so S matches \(4\). These descriptions are connected by the same direction criterion. The vocabulary changes because the particle-motion geometry changes.

question: Two waves travel toward the east through different media. In wave I, particles move north-south. In wave II, particles move east-west. The correct classification is
opt_a: wave I is longitudinal and wave II is transverse
opt_b: wave I is transverse and wave II is longitudinal
explanation:
\( \textbf{Propagation direction:} \) Both waves travel toward the east.
\( \textbf{Wave I particle motion:} \) North-south motion is perpendicular to east-west propagation.
\( \textbf{Classification of wave I:} \) Perpendicular particle motion means wave I is transverse.
\( \textbf{Wave II particle motion:} \) East-west motion is along the same line as the propagation direction.
\( \textbf{Classification of wave II:} \) Parallel particle motion means wave II is longitudinal.
\( \textbf{Option decision:} \) The matching choice is transverse for wave I and longitudinal for wave II.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) Wave I is transverse and wave II is longitudinal.
The words east, west, north, and south are only direction markers; the classification comes from parallel or perpendicular comparison.

question: A description says, “A wave has compressions and rarefactions, so its particles move perpendicular to the direction of propagation.” The part needing correction is that
opt_a: compressions and rarefactions indicate parallel particle motion
opt_b: compressions and rarefactions occur only in electromagnetic waves
opt_c: particle motion is absent in all longitudinal waves
opt_d: perpendicular particle motion produces pressure maxima in every medium
explanation: Compressions and rarefactions are characteristic of longitudinal waves. They occur when particles of the medium move back and forth parallel to the direction of wave propagation. This motion alternately crowds and spreads the particles. Perpendicular particle motion is the feature of transverse waves, where crests and troughs are the usual displacement features. The statement correctly recognizes compression-rarefaction language but attaches it to the wrong direction relation. Correcting the direction relation repairs the classification.

question:
The following statements compare transverse and longitudinal waves.
I. Transverse waves involve particle displacement perpendicular to propagation.
II. Longitudinal waves involve particle displacement parallel to propagation.
III. Only longitudinal waves can transfer energy.
IV. Sound in air is a common example of a longitudinal wave.
The supported set is
explanation: Statement I is correct because perpendicular displacement defines a transverse wave. Statement II is correct because parallel displacement defines a longitudinal wave. Statement IV is also correct because sound in air travels by compressions and rarefactions. Statement III is not correct because both transverse and longitudinal waves can transfer energy. A wave on a string can carry energy along the string even though it is transverse. Energy transfer is a general wave feature, while transverse and longitudinal labels describe particle-motion direction.

question: A displacement-position graph of a transverse wave shows a crest-to-crest separation of \(0.60\,\text{m}\). A pressure-position graph of a longitudinal sound wave shows a compression-to-compression separation of \(0.60\,\text{m}\). The two separations represent
explanation: In a transverse wave, the distance between two nearest crests is one wavelength. In a longitudinal pressure wave, the distance between two nearest compressions is also one wavelength. Both pairs are nearest points in the same phase of their respective wave patterns. The visual features differ because one graph uses crests and troughs while the other uses pressure maxima and minima. Amplitude is measured by maximum displacement or pressure variation from the mean, not by spacing between repeated features. The same wavelength idea can appear through different physical representations.

question: A narrow spring is used in two demonstrations. In Case 1, the hand moves the end of the spring up and down while the pulse travels along the spring. In Case 2, the hand pushes and pulls the end along the length of the spring. The likely wave types are
explanation: In Case 1, the end of the spring is moved up and down while the disturbance travels along the length of the spring. The particle displacement is perpendicular to the direction of propagation, so the pulse is transverse. In Case 2, the hand pushes and pulls along the spring’s length. The coils move back and forth parallel to the direction in which the disturbance travels, producing compressions and rarefactions. That makes Case 2 longitudinal. The same spring can be used to demonstrate different wave types depending on how the disturbance is produced. The direction of the hand’s motion relative to the propagation direction decides the classification.

question:
A table compares common features of two wave representations. Select the row that is mismatched.
RowWave representationFeature
PTransverse displacement waveCrests and troughs
QLongitudinal pressure waveCompressions and rarefactions
RSound in airLongitudinal mechanical wave
SLongitudinal waveParticle displacement always perpendicular to propagation
explanation: Row S is mismatched because a longitudinal wave has particle displacement parallel to the direction of propagation. Perpendicular particle displacement is the defining feature of a transverse wave. Row P is suitable because crests and troughs are used in a transverse displacement representation. Row Q is suitable because compressions and rarefactions are natural features of a longitudinal pressure wave. Row R is suitable because sound in air is a longitudinal mechanical wave. The mismatch is a direction error, not a naming error.

question: A learner sees alternate dark and light bands in a spring photograph. The dark bands are regions where coils are crowded, and the light bands are regions where coils are spread out. The photograph most directly represents
opt_a: a longitudinal wave with compressions and rarefactions
opt_b: a transverse wave with crests, troughs, and no compressions
opt_d: a standing wave with no particle motion anywhere
explanation: Crowded coil regions in a spring represent compressions. Spread-out coil regions represent rarefactions. These features occur when the coils move back and forth along the length of the spring, which is longitudinal motion. A transverse wave would usually be represented by displacement above and below a mean line, giving crests and troughs. The photograph describes changes in spacing along the direction of propagation rather than vertical displacement. The dark-light pattern is therefore a compression-rarefaction representation.

question: A wave has wavelength \(0.75\,\text{m}\). In one representation, this is the distance from one crest to the next crest. In another representation of a sound wave, the same wavelength would be the distance from
opt_a: one compression to the nearest rarefaction
opt_b: the mean line to a crest
opt_c: one particle’s extreme displacement to its mean position
opt_d: one compression to the next compression
explanation: Wavelength is the distance between nearest points that are in the same phase. In a transverse wave, one crest to the next crest gives one wavelength. In a longitudinal sound wave, one compression to the next compression gives the same kind of spatial repeat. A compression to the nearest rarefaction corresponds to opposite stages of the pressure variation, so it represents half a wavelength in a regular sinusoidal wave. The mean line to a crest gives amplitude in a transverse displacement graph. The definition of wavelength stays the same even when the visible features change.

question: A single upward jerk is given to one end of a stretched rope. The disturbance travels along the rope only once. This disturbance is best called
explanation: A pulse is a single, short-lived disturbance that travels through a medium. In this situation, the rope end is jerked once, so only one disturbance is produced. A periodic wave would require repeated oscillations of the source at regular intervals. A standing wave involves a fixed pattern of nodes and antinodes, which is not described here. Beats require superposition of two waves of nearly equal frequencies. The single-jerk condition is what separates a pulse from a continuous wave train.

question: A hand moves the end of a string up and down regularly many times. The disturbance produced on the string is more likely to be
opt_a: a repeated wave train on the string
opt_c: a motion with no energy transfer
opt_d: a permanent flow of string material
explanation: Repeated up-and-down motion of the source produces repeated disturbances in the string. These disturbances form a periodic wave or wave train. In a transverse string wave, the repeated high and low parts are described as crests and troughs. A single pulse would be produced by only one brief disturbance, not by repeated oscillations. The string material does not flow permanently along the string; each part of the string mainly oscillates about its mean position. The regular repetition of the source is the reason the pattern repeats in space and time.

question:
The following observations are made for two disturbances on the same stretched string.
I. Disturbance P is produced by one quick jerk.
II. Disturbance Q is produced by regular repeated motion of the hand.
III. Both disturbances travel along the same string under the same tension.
The most suitable conclusion is
opt_a: P is a periodic wave and Q is a pulse
opt_b: P is a pulse and Q is a periodic wave
opt_c: P cannot carry energy but Q can carry energy
opt_d: P must travel through vacuum but Q needs a string
explanation: A single quick jerk produces one travelling disturbance, so P is a pulse. Regular repeated motion produces a train of disturbances, so Q is a periodic wave. Both can carry energy along the string. Both require the string as the material medium because these are mechanical waves. The fact that they are on the same stretched string tells us they share the same kind of medium, not that one becomes non-mechanical. The difference between them comes from how the source is disturbed: once or repeatedly.

question: A pulse and a periodic wave are sent separately along the same uniform string without changing the tension. The most reasonable statement about their speeds is
opt_a: the pulse must be slower because it has no wavelength
opt_b: the periodic wave must be faster because it has many crests
opt_c: their speeds are decided mainly by the same string conditions
opt_d: the speed becomes zero for the pulse after one oscillation
explanation: In a given uniform string under the same tension, the speed of a transverse disturbance is determined by the properties of the string and its tension. A pulse is a single disturbance, while a periodic wave is a repeated disturbance, but both propagate through the same medium. Having many crests does not by itself make a periodic wave faster. A pulse also carries energy and can travel through the string. Later, the speed of a string wave is expressed using the string tension and linear mass density. The source pattern affects whether the disturbance is single or repeated, but the medium controls the propagation speed.

question:
Use the graph description below.
Graph P shows one isolated bump travelling along a string. Graph Q shows a repeated sinusoidal pattern extending along the string.
The better identification of Graph P and Graph Q is
opt_a: P is a periodic wave, Q is a pulse
opt_b: P is a pulse, Q is a periodic wave
opt_c: P is a standing wave, Q is a sound wave in vacuum
opt_d: P is a compression, Q is a rarefaction
explanation: One isolated bump represents a pulse because it is a single travelling disturbance. A repeated sinusoidal pattern represents a periodic wave because the same shape repeats again and again. The graph description is a spatial snapshot, so it shows how the disturbance is distributed along the string at one instant. A standing wave would have fixed nodes and antinodes rather than a single travelling bump or a travelling repeated pattern. Compressions and rarefactions belong to longitudinal waves, not to the crest-shaped string graph described here. The number of repeated spatial units is the main clue.

question:
Match the descriptions with the suitable terms.
DescriptionTerm
P. One short travelling disturbance1. Pulse
Q. Repeated disturbance produced regularly2. Periodic wave
R. Repeated sinusoidal disturbance along a medium3. Wave train
S. Shape of disturbance at one instant4. Wave profile
explanation: A pulse is one short travelling disturbance, so P matches \(1\). A periodic wave is produced by repeated disturbance of the source, so Q matches \(2\). A wave train is a sequence of repeated wave disturbances, often represented by a sinusoidal pattern, so R matches \(3\). The shape of the disturbance at a particular instant is called the wave profile, so S matches \(4\). These terms describe different ways a disturbance may appear or repeat. The main separation is between a single disturbance and a regularly repeating one.

question: A periodic wave on a string has speed \(8.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). A pulse is then sent along the same string without changing the string tension or the string itself. The pulse travels \(4.0\,\text{m}\). How much time should it take?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) The same string conditions are maintained, so the pulse speed is \(8.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Distance travelled by pulse:} \) \(s=4.0\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Time \(t\).
\( \textbf{Relation for propagation:} \)
\[
v=\frac{s}{t}
\]
This relation is applied to the travelling disturbance along the string.
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
t=\frac{s}{v}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
t=\frac{4.0\,\text{m}}{8.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
t=0.50\,\text{s}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The pulse should take \(0.50\,\text{s}\).
The pulse is not made slower merely because it is not a repeated wave train.

question: A sinusoidal wave is called periodic because
opt_a: its pattern repeats in space and time
opt_b: it contains only one isolated disturbance
opt_c: the particles of the medium are permanently transported
opt_d: it can exist only in vacuum
explanation: A sinusoidal wave has a smoothly repeating pattern. At a fixed instant, the shape repeats after each wavelength \(\lambda\) along space. At a fixed position, the motion repeats after each time period \(T\). This repeated behaviour is why the wave is called periodic. A single isolated disturbance is a pulse, not a periodic wave. Periodicity describes repetition of the disturbance pattern, not permanent transport of the medium.

question: A wave train is shown on a string. Three neighbouring crests are marked P, Q, and R in order along the direction of propagation. If the distance from P to Q is \(0.30\,\text{m}\), the distance from P to R is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) P, Q, and R are neighbouring crests in order.
\( \textbf{Crest-to-crest spacing:} \) The distance between neighbouring crests is one wavelength.
\[
PQ=\lambda=0.30\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Required distance:} \) P to R covers two crest-to-crest intervals.
\[
PR=PQ+QR
\]
Since Q and R are also neighbouring crests,
\[
QR=\lambda=0.30\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
PR=0.30\,\text{m}+0.30\,\text{m}=0.60\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The distance from P to R is \(0.60\,\text{m}\).
The distance from a crest to the next crest is already one full wavelength, not half a wavelength.

question: A crest in a transverse wave represents
opt_a: maximum positive displacement from the mean position
opt_b: maximum negative displacement from the mean position
opt_c: maximum pressure in every kind of wave
explanation: In a transverse displacement representation, a crest is the highest point of the wave profile. It corresponds to maximum positive displacement from the mean position. A trough corresponds to maximum negative displacement. Pressure maxima are described as compressions in a longitudinal sound wave, not as crests in the basic displacement picture. A crest is not a point of zero displacement. The sign of displacement depends on the chosen vertical direction, but the crest is the positive extreme in the usual drawing.

question: A trough in a transverse wave is related to the mean position in the same way that
opt_a: a rarefaction is related to higher density
opt_b: a crest is related to zero displacement
opt_d: a compression is related to no pressure change
explanation: A trough is the lowest point of a transverse wave profile. It represents maximum negative displacement from the mean position. This is opposite in sign to a crest, which represents maximum positive displacement. A rarefaction is a low-pressure, low-density region, so it is not related to higher density. A compression is associated with higher pressure and density, not with no pressure change. The trough is best understood as one extreme of displacement about equilibrium.

question: In a longitudinal sound wave, the distance between a compression and the nearest rarefaction is \(0.25\,\text{m}\). What is the wavelength of the sound?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given information:} \) Distance from a compression to the nearest rarefaction is \(0.25\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Wave pattern idea:} \) A compression and the nearest rarefaction are opposite stages of the pressure variation.
\( \textbf{Spacing relation:} \)
\[
\text{compression to nearest rarefaction}=\frac{\lambda}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\frac{\lambda}{2}=0.25\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Solving for wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda=2(0.25\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda=0.50\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength is \(0.50\,\text{m}\).
A compression-to-compression distance would be one wavelength, but compression-to-nearest-rarefaction is only half of that.

question:
Study the table and select the row with a mismatched description.
RowFeatureDescription
PCrestMaximum positive displacement
QTroughMaximum negative displacement
RCompressionHigh pressure and high density
SRarefactionHigh pressure and high density
explanation: Rarefaction is a region where the particles of the medium are more spread out than usual. Therefore, it corresponds to lower pressure and lower density, not high pressure and high density. Row P is suitable because a crest is maximum positive displacement in a transverse displacement wave. Row Q is suitable because a trough is maximum negative displacement. Row R is suitable because a compression is a crowded region with higher pressure and density. The mismatched row confuses rarefaction with compression.

question: A sound wave travels through air. At one point, the pressure is momentarily lower than the normal pressure, and the air particles are more spread out than usual. This point is in a
explanation: In a longitudinal sound wave, a rarefaction is a region of lower pressure and lower density. The air particles are farther apart than in the undisturbed state. A compression would have higher pressure and higher density because particles are closer together. Crests and troughs are more suitable for transverse displacement descriptions, not for the pressure-density description of sound in air. The condition “more spread out than usual” identifies a rarefaction directly. The pressure and density clues point to the same region.

question: The spacing between successive similar features in a periodic wave is interpreted using phase. For a transverse displacement wave, the nearest similar feature after a crest is
opt_c: the mean position just after the crest
explanation: Wavelength is the distance between nearest points in the same phase. In a transverse displacement wave, two neighbouring crests are in the same phase because both represent maximum positive displacement. A crest and the nearest trough are opposite extremes, so they are not in the same phase. A mean-position point near a crest is also at a different stage of oscillation. Compression belongs to a longitudinal pressure representation, not to the crest-trough description of this transverse wave. The next crest gives one full spatial repeat of the transverse pattern.

question:
The pressure pattern in a sound wave is observed along a straight line.
Point P is a compression. Moving in the direction of propagation, point Q is the nearest rarefaction, and point R is the next compression after Q.
If \(PQ=0.18\,\text{m}\), what is \(PR\)?
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given arrangement:} \) P is a compression, Q is the nearest rarefaction, and R is the next compression.
\( \textbf{Compression to nearest rarefaction:} \)
\[
PQ=\frac{\lambda}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Given value:} \)
\[
PQ=0.18\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Finding wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda=2PQ
\]
